name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q01 - Estimated age of the universe Big Bang

questiontext.text: According to the Big Bang theory, approximately how old is the universe?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The Big Bang theory attempts to explain the origin of the universe as a singular huge explosion in physical terms.

Step 2:
Following this expansion, the universe cooled, and hydrogen and helium formed as galaxies condensed under gravitation.

Step 3:
The textbook explicitly states that the universe is very old, almost 13.8 billion years old.

Final Answer:
The estimated age of the universe is almost 13.8 billion years.

answer.text: Almost 4.5 billion years
Almost 13.8 billion years
Almost 4.0 billion years
Almost 2000 million years

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q02 - Atmospheric conditions present on primitive Earth

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the gaseous composition and nature of the atmosphere on early Earth before the origin of life?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
On early Earth, there was no free oxygen; hence, the atmosphere was reducing in nature.

Step 2:
Volcanic outgassing and the molten surface released water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide, and ammonia, which covered the surface.

Step 3:
Free molecular oxygen was absent until water vapour was later split by solar ultraviolet radiation and early photosynthetic organisms evolved.

Final Answer:
The primitive atmosphere was reducing and composed of water vapour, methane, ammonia, and carbon dioxide without free molecular oxygen.

answer.text: Reducing atmosphere composed predominantly of free oxygen, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen
Oxidising atmosphere containing abundant free oxygen, nitrogen, and ozone
Reducing atmosphere containing water vapour, methane, ammonia, and carbon dioxide without free oxygen
Oxidising atmosphere with high levels of methane, ammonia, and molecular nitrogen

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q03 - Temperature and gases in Miller reaction flask

questiontext.text: In his famous 1953 simulation experiment on chemical evolution, S.L. Miller created an electric spark discharge in a closed flask containing which mixture of gases at what temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
S.L. Miller set up a laboratory apparatus to recreate the prebiotic atmospheric conditions postulated by Oparin and Haldane.

Step 2:
He circulated a gaseous mixture of methane (\(\text{CH}_4\)), hydrogen (\(\text{H}_2\)), ammonia (\(\text{NH}_3\)), and water vapour.

Step 3:
The reaction flask with tungsten electrodes was maintained at an electric discharge temperature of \(800^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Answer:
The mixture consisted of \(\text{CH}_4\), \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{NH}_3\), and water vapour at \(800^\circ\text{C}\).

answer.text: \(\text{CH}_4\), \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{NH}_3\), and liquid water at \(80^\circ\text{C}\)
\(\text{CH}_4\), \(\text{O}_2\), \(\text{NH}_3\), and water vapour at \(800^\circ\text{C}\)
\(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{N}_2\), and water vapour at \(100^\circ\text{C}\)
\(\text{CH}_4\), \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{NH}_3\), and water vapour at \(800^\circ\text{C}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q04 - Molecules synthesized during primitive simulation chemical experiments

questiontext.text: What specific organic compounds were directly observed by S.L. Miller in his spark discharge experiment, and what additional molecules were synthesized by other scientists using similar prebiotic setups?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Analysis of the fluid collected in the condenser trap of Miller's experiment revealed the formation of simple amino acids.

Step 2:
In similar follow-up experiments by other researchers using modified primitive reducing atmospheres, sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments, and fats were also produced.

Step 3:
These observations supported the hypothesis of chemical evolution, demonstrating that biological micromolecules could arise spontaneously from inorganic precursors.

Final Answer:
Miller directly observed amino acids, while subsequent experiments formed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments, and fats.

answer.text: Miller observed DNA and RNA; others observed intact cellular organelles and membranes
Miller observed polypeptide enzymes; others observed self-replicating viral particles
Miller observed amino acids; others observed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments, and fats
Miller observed complex polysaccharides; others observed only inorganic salts and ammonia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q05 - Pasteur experimental demonstration against spontaneous generation

questiontext.text: How did Louis Pasteur conclusively disprove the long-held theory of spontaneous generation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The theory of spontaneous generation proposed that living organisms could arise spontaneously from non-living or decaying matter such as mud and straw.

Step 2:
Louis Pasteur prepared nutrient broth in pre-sterilised swan-neck flasks.

Step 3:
He demonstrated that in a closed, pre-sterilised flask, no living organisms arose from killed yeast, whereas in an open flask exposed to airborne organisms, new living organisms appeared.

Step 4:
This proved conclusively that living organisms arise solely from pre-existing living cells (biogenesis).

Final Answer:
By showing that living organisms arose from killed yeast only in flasks open to air, but not in pre-sterilised sealed flasks.

answer.text: By synthesizing living yeast cells directly from inorganic minerals in an open crucible
By freezing decaying organic straw to halt bacterial division permanently
By observing that autoclaved broth in airtight flasks generated bacterial colonies after exposure to sunlight
By demonstrating that life did not come from killed yeast in pre-sterilised sealed flasks, but only in flasks open to air

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q06 - Timeline for noncellular and cellular life forms

questiontext.text: According to geological records and evolutionary biology, when did the first non-cellular forms of life and the first cellular forms of life originate on Earth, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Following the formation of Earth approximately 4.5 billion years ago, life first appeared around 4 billion years ago.

Step 2:
The first non-cellular forms of life, comprising giant macromolecular capsules of RNA, proteins, and polysaccharides, could have originated about 3 billion years ago (3000 million years ago).

Step 3:
The first cellular forms of life did not originate until about 2000 million years ago (2 billion years ago), and these early cells were aquatic single-celled organisms.

Final Answer:
Non-cellular life arose around 3 billion years ago, and cellular life arose around 2000 million years ago.

answer.text: 2000 million years ago for non-cellular life and 500 million years ago for cellular life
500 million years ago for non-cellular life and 350 million years ago for cellular life
4.5 billion years ago for non-cellular life and 3.5 billion years ago for cellular life
3 billion years ago for non-cellular life and 2000 million years ago for cellular life

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q07 - Extraterrestrial transfer of life spores concept panspermia

questiontext.text: The hypothesis favored by some astronomers and early Greek thinkers that units of life called 'spores' were transferred from outer space to different planets, including Earth, is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Early Greek philosophers and some subsequent astronomers considered that life was not initially generated on Earth.

Step 2:
Instead, resistant reproductive units or spores were envisioned as travelling across stellar space to seed various planets.

Step 3:
This concept of cosmic interplanetary seeding is specifically called panspermia.

Final Answer:
The concept of extraterrestrial transfer of life spores is known as panspermia.

answer.text: Abiogenesis
Biopoiesis
Spontaneous generation
Panspermia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q08 - Solar ultraviolet photolysis and primitive ocean formation

questiontext.text: What crucial sequence of events led to the condensation of water vapour and formation of oceans on the cooling primitive Earth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
On the primitive hot Earth without an ozone screen, solar ultraviolet radiation penetrated directly to the surface.

Step 2:
Ultraviolet rays broke water vapour into hydrogen and oxygen; the lighter hydrogen gas escaped into space.

Step 3:
Free oxygen reacted with ammonia and methane to produce water, carbon dioxide, and other oxidised compounds, while the protective ozone layer gradually formed.

Step 4:
As the planet cooled, atmospheric water vapour condensed and fell as torrential rains, filling depressions on the crust to form primitive oceans.

Final Answer:
Solar ultraviolet rays split water into hydrogen and oxygen; escaping hydrogen allowed oxygen to form oxides, and subsequent cooling condensed water into torrential rains that filled crustal depressions.

answer.text: Infrared rays combined methane and oxygen into liquid water, which directly erupted from mantle fissures
Ozone breakdown released heavy hydrogen that reacted with volcanic dust to produce subterranean condensation
Ultraviolet rays split water into hydrogen and oxygen; lighter hydrogen escaped, and cooling condensed water vapour into rain that filled surface depressions
Atmospheric carbon dioxide condensed directly at freezing temperatures to melt crustal rocks into liquid water

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q09 - Postulates of traditional special creation theory

questiontext.text: The traditional theory of special creation encompasses three major connotations. Which of the following correctly includes these three connotations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The theory of special creation is rooted in conventional religious literature and asserts three explicit premises.

Step 2:
First, all living organisms (species or types) visible today were created as such without changing.

Step 3:
Second, biological diversity has always remained the same since the moment of creation and will remain unchanged in the future.

Step 4:
Third, the Earth is relatively young, being only about 4000 years old.

Final Answer:
The three connotations state that all existing species were created as such, diversity was always the same and will remain so, and the Earth is approximately 4000 years old.

answer.text: All organisms originated in oceans, acquired traits through use and disuse, and Earth is 13.8 billion years old
New species arise exclusively through saltation, diversity increases exponentially, and Earth is 4.5 billion years old
All species were created as such, diversity has remained and will remain constant, and Earth is about 4000 years old
Species evolved gradually from common ancestors, diversity fluctuated constantly, and Earth is billions of years old

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q10 - Darwinian definition of evolutionary fitness of populations

questiontext.text: In Darwinian evolutionary theory, the fitness of an individual or population ultimately and strictly refers to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Charles Darwin observed that populations possess built-in variations that affect survival under varying environmental conditions.

Step 2:
However, physical prowess, strength, or individual longevity alone do not determine evolutionary success unless translated into progeny.

Step 3:
Darwin explicitly asserted that fitness in the evolutionary sense refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness, meaning the capacity to survive and leave more fertile offspring in the next generation.

Final Answer:
Darwinian fitness refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness.

answer.text: Individual lifespan and resistance to senescence irrespective of offspring count
Physical muscular strength and fighting capacity alone
Physiological tolerance to starvation without successful reproduction
Reproductive fitness and the ability to leave more progeny

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q11 - Geographical location of Wallace evolutionary conclusions work

questiontext.text: Alfred Russel Wallace, a contemporary naturalist who independently arrived at conclusions regarding natural selection similar to Darwin's, conducted his fieldwork in which geographical region?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Charles Darwin formulated his evolutionary concepts following his voyage on the H.M.S. Beagle.

Step 2:
Around the same time, Alfred Russel Wallace studied biogeography, species distribution, and natural selection.

Step 3:
Wallace carried out his extensive naturalist observations and collections in the Malay Archipelago.

Final Answer:
Alfred Russel Wallace worked in the Malay Archipelago.

answer.text: Madagascar Island
Hawaiian Archipelago
Malay Archipelago
Galapagos Islands

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q12 - Two fundamental key concepts of Darwinian evolution

questiontext.text: What are the two foundational key concepts of the Darwinian theory of evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The Darwinian framework explains the pattern and mechanism of biological evolution using two central ideas.

Step 2:
The pattern of evolution involves descent with modification from common ancestors, termed branching descent.

Step 3:
The primary mechanism driving this adaptation and diversification is natural selection operating on heritable variations.

Final Answer:
The two key concepts are branching descent and natural selection.

answer.text: Branching descent and natural selection
Saltation and single-step large mutations
Genetic drift and reproductive isolation without variation
Use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired characters

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q13 - Influence of Malthusian demographic principles on Darwin

questiontext.text: How did Thomas Malthus's essay on human populations fundamentally influence Charles Darwin's conception of natural selection?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Thomas Malthus highlighted that populations have the reproductive capacity to increase exponentially if unchecked, while natural resources remain limited.

Step 2:
Darwin realized that in nature, despite theoretical exponential reproductive capacity, real population sizes generally remain stable over time (except for seasonal fluctuations).

Step 3:
This discrepancy implied an intense competition for limited resources, where individuals possessing advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce preferentially.

Final Answer:
By highlighting that population capacity for exponential growth alongside limited resources creates intense competition where only adapted variants survive.

answer.text: By demonstrating that geological sedimentary strata correspond directly to worldwide catastrophic floods
By proposing that environmental changes induce targeted non-random mutations directly in reproductive gametes
By proving that all organisms possess an innate conscious drive toward morphological perfection
By showing that limited natural resources and potential exponential population growth lead to competition for survival

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q14 - Paleontological evidence from stratified sedimentary rocks

questiontext.text: How does the examination of fossils within successive sedimentary rock layers provide paleontological evidence for organic evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Sedimentary rocks form through sequential deposition of sediments over geological eras, with deeper layers representing older periods.

Step 2:
Fossils preserved within specific sedimentary layers reveal that life forms varied across time and that certain organisms were restricted to specific geological intervals.

Step 3:
The temporal progression of forms demonstrates that new types of organisms arose at different times in Earth's history rather than appearing simultaneously.

Final Answer:
Fossils in different aged strata show that life forms varied over time and that distinct life forms were restricted to specific geological time spans.

answer.text: Sedimentation rates indicate that all major animal phyla originated simultaneously within the past 4000 years
Fossils in deeper strata invariably possess larger brains and greater structural complexity than those in upper strata
Fossils in different aged rock strata demonstrate that life forms changed over time and were restricted to specific geological periods
Every sedimentary layer contains an identical assortment of modern and primitive fossilized organisms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q15 - Rebuttal of Haeckel biogenetic proposal by Baer

questiontext.text: Ernst Haeckel proposed embryological support for evolution, which was subsequently discredited by Karl Ernst von Baer. What specific critical observation did von Baer make that disproved Haeckel's proposal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Ernst Haeckel proposed the biogenetic law, suggesting that the embryonic stages of an organism retrace the adult forms of its evolutionary ancestors.

Step 2:
For instance, Haeckel cited the transient appearance of pharyngeal gill slits in mammalian and human embryos as recapitulating an adult fish stage.

Step 3:
Karl Ernst von Baer conducted rigorous comparative embryological studies and demonstrated that embryos of higher vertebrates never pass through the adult stages of other, more ancestral animals; rather, embryos merely share general early embryonic characteristics.

Final Answer:
Von Baer observed that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

answer.text: Embryonic developmental trajectories are completely independent of common genetic ancestry
Vertebrate embryos lack vestigial gill slits at all developmental stages
Embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals
Fish embryos exhibit mammalian limb buds during blastula formation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q16 - Relationship between homologous structures and divergent evolution

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly characterizes homologous organs and their evolutionary significance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Homology refers to structural similarity arising from common developmental origin and shared ancestry.

Step 2:
Although homologous structures perform different functions in different species due to adaptations to varied environmental demands or niches, their fundamental anatomical blueprint remains identical.

Step 3:
This evolutionary trajectory—wherein the same basic ancestral structure diversifies along different functional paths—is called divergent evolution.

Final Answer:
Homologous organs share a common anatomical origin and basic architecture but perform different functions due to divergent evolution.

answer.text: They represent superficial adaptations in unrelated organisms living in identical habitats
They perform identical biological functions through convergent evolution despite having unrelated embryonic origins
They lack any underlying skeletal similarity but develop in response to identical nutritional requirements
They share similar anatomical architecture indicating common ancestry, but perform different functions through divergent evolution

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q17 - Skeletal pattern in forelimbs of diverse mammals

questiontext.text: The forelimbs of humans, cheetahs, whales, and bats perform grasping, running, swimming, and flying, respectively. Which anatomical evidence confirms that these forelimbs are homologous organs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Despite vastly different external morphologies and specialised functions, the internal skeletal organisation of these mammalian forelimbs is identical.

Step 2:
Each possesses the same basic set and arrangement of bones: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges.

Step 3:
This shared structural framework reflects common mammalian ancestry and represents a classic example of divergent evolution.

Final Answer:
All of them share the same anatomical arrangement of bones, including humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges.

answer.text: They are formed by identical muscular contractions without possessing an internal bony skeleton
They share the same skeletal plan comprising humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges
They develop from different embryonic germ layers to achieve identical functional efficiency
They lack carpals and phalanges in swimming and flying forms but retain identical skin coverings

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q18 - Homology exhibited by thorn and tendril structures

questiontext.text: In botany, the thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita represent homologous structures because both:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The thorn of Bougainvillea provides protection, whereas the tendril of Cucurbita aids in climbing.

Step 2:
Despite performing different functions, morphological and anatomical studies show that both structures originate as modified axillary buds.

Step 3:
Shared structural origin and position with divergence into different functions constitutes homology based on divergent evolution.

Final Answer:
Both are modified axillary buds representing homology through divergent evolution.

answer.text: Develop from adventitious roots to store water and starches
Represent analogous modifications derived from distinct floral whorls
Originate from leaf laminae and perform identical photosynthetic functions
Originate from axillary buds but have diverged to perform different functions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q19 - Convergent evolution leading to analogous anatomical structures

questiontext.text: Analogous organs arise when unrelated groups of organisms evolve structurally distinct organs that perform similar functions. What primary evolutionary force drives this convergent evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Analogy is the opposite of homology; analogous organs are anatomically dissimilar and do not share a common ancestral origin.

Step 2:
When different lineages inhabit similar ecological niches or encounter common environmental challenges, natural selection favors similar functional adaptations.

Step 3:
Thus, adaptation to similar habitats and functional needs results in convergent evolution.

Final Answer:
Similar environmental demands and habitats select for similar functional adaptations in distinct lineages.

answer.text: Inheritance of identical unmodified genetic sequences from a recent common ancestor
Selection of similar adaptive features in different groups due to common habitat demands
Random genetic drift occurring exclusively in isolated island populations
Spontaneous macroscopic chromosomal translocations occurring simultaneously in unrelated species

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q20 - Evaluating analogous structures representing convergent evolutionary paths

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of anatomical structures represents analogy resulting from convergent evolution rather than homology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Homologous structures share common ancestry and developmental origin (such as mammalian forelimbs or vertebrate hearts).

Step 2:
Analogous structures perform similar functions despite differing in anatomical origin and structure.

Step 3:
The eye of the octopus (a cephalopod mollusc) and the eye of a mammal (a vertebrate) perform identical visual functions, yet their retinal architecture and embryonic development differ fundamentally.

Step 4:
Similarly, the flippers of penguins (birds) and dolphins (mammals) are analogous structures adapted for aquatic propulsion.

Final Answer:
The eye of the octopus and the eye of mammals represent analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution.

answer.text: Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita
Eye of the octopus and eye of mammals
Forelimbs of cheetah and forelimbs of whale
Vertebrate hearts and vertebrate brains

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q21 - Storage organ analogy in sweet potato potato

questiontext.text: Sweet potato and potato both serve as underground food storage organs, yet they are cited as classic examples of analogy. What is the anatomical basis for this classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is an underground root modification adapted for nutrient storage.

Step 2:
Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is an underground stem modification (tuber) bearing nodes and buds.

Step 3:
Because their anatomical origins are completely different (root vs stem) while performing the same functional role (food storage), they represent analogous organs resulting from convergent evolution.

Final Answer:
Sweet potato is a modified root, whereas potato is a modified stem, making them analogous organs.

answer.text: Sweet potato is a root modification, whereas potato is a stem modification
Both represent homologous swollen hypocotyl structures sharing identical nodal patterns
Both are derived exclusively from leaf petioles that store starches in identical vascular bundles
Sweet potato is an aerial stem modification, whereas potato is an adventitious root tuber

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q22 - Biochemical similarities pointing toward shared biological ancestry

questiontext.text: How do comparative biochemical studies of proteins and metabolic genes across diverse organisms provide compelling evidence for evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Comparative biochemistry examines the molecular sequences of essential proteins and genes across diverse taxa.

Step 2:
Organisms that perform identical fundamental biochemical functions possess remarkably conserved amino acid and nucleotide sequences.

Step 3:
Just as comparative structural anatomy indicates shared morphological ancestry, these biochemical similarities point directly to a shared common ancestor from which modern diversity arose.

Final Answer:
Biochemical similarities in functional proteins and genes indicate common evolutionary ancestry just as anatomical homologies do.

answer.text: Biochemical pathways are completely unique to each species, proving independent creation of all taxa
Only photosynthetic plants share metabolic enzymes, whereas animals lack all homologous proteins
Differences in genetic codes prove that cellular life originated independently in every geological epoch
Similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function point to common ancestry among diverse organisms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q23 - Shift in peppered moth proportions post industrialisation

questiontext.text: In England, collections of the peppered moth (Biston betularia) revealed a predominance of white-winged moths in the 1850s, whereas dark-winged (melanised) moths dominated by 1920. What selective mechanism drove this shift?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Before industrialisation in the 1850s, tree trunks were encrusted with thick, light-coloured lichens, providing camouflage for white-winged moths against predatory birds.

Step 2:
With widespread industrialisation by 1920, industrial smoke and soot blackened the tree trunks, and sensitive lichens disappeared.

Step 3:
Against the darkened bark, white-winged moths were easily spotted and predated by birds, whereas dark-winged melanic variants were camouflaged, survived better, and left more progeny, leading to directional natural selection.

Final Answer:
Tree trunks blackened by soot allowed dark-winged moths to camouflage better against predators, whereas white-winged moths were preferentially predated.

answer.text: Dark-winged moths migrated from tropical continents and physically killed the resident white-winged population
Industrial coal smoke acted as a physiological mutagen that converted adult white wings into black wings directly
Soot-blackened tree trunks provided camouflage for melanic moths, while white-winged moths were preferentially spotted and eaten by predators
White-winged moths laid eggs exclusively on factory chimneys where high temperatures prevented hatching

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q24 - Sensitivity of lichens as industrial pollution indicators

questiontext.text: Why did the presence or absence of lichens on tree bark play a pivotal role in the natural selection of peppered moths in England?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Lichens consist of a symbiotic association between algae and fungi that are exquisitely sensitive to atmospheric air pollutants, especially sulfur dioxide.

Step 2:
Consequently, lichens cannot grow in polluted industrial areas and serve as biological pollution indicators.

Step 3:
In unpolluted rural areas, dense white lichen growth camouflaged light-winged moths, but in polluted urban areas, the absence of lichens combined with soot accumulation exposed light-winged moths to heavy predation.

Final Answer:
Lichens do not grow in polluted areas; their absence and soot deposition exposed white moths to predators.

answer.text: Lichens emit intense fluorescence that repels avian predators only when illuminated by industrial streetlights
Lichens are sensitive to pollution and do not grow in industrial areas, exposing white moths against dark tree bark
Lichens secrete toxic enzymes that kill dark-winged caterpillars exclusively during winter
Lichens provide the exclusive food source for adult moths, forcing melanic moths to starve in unpolluted zones

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q25 - Evolution of antibiotic resistance through anthropogenic action

questiontext.text: The rapid emergence of pesticide-resistant insects and antibiotic-resistant bacteria within months or years rather than centuries exemplifies evolution driven by anthropogenic action. What fundamental truth about evolution does this demonstrate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Human activities—such as excessive application of chemical pesticides, herbicides, and antibiotics—create strong, novel selective pressures.

Step 2:
In any pre-existing mixed microbial or insect population, rare pre-existing resistant variants (conferred by chance mutations) survive the chemical exposure and reproduce, rapidly increasing in frequency.

Step 3:
This demonstrates that evolution is not a directed, teleological, or deterministic process; rather, it is a stochastic process governed by chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms.

Final Answer:
Evolution is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms.

answer.text: Chemical exposure causes directed mutations specifically tailored to metabolize the applied antibiotic
Evolution is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms
Resistance arises because organisms consciously modify their genetic code in response to physiological stress
Evolution is a strictly deterministic and goal-oriented process guided toward organismal perfection

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q26 - Defining process of geographical adaptive radiation

questiontext.text: The evolutionary process wherein different species arise within a given geographical area, starting from a common ancestral point and radiating into diverse ecological niches and habitats, is defined as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Adaptive radiation describes the diversification of an ancestral lineage into an array of species specialized for different lifestyles and ecological roles.

Step 2:
This occurs when descendants colonize an area with varied unoccupied niches or habitats.

Step 3:
Classic textbook examples include Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands and Australian marsupials.

Final Answer:
This evolutionary diversification is defined as adaptive radiation.

answer.text: Adaptive radiation
Convergent evolution
Saltational speciation
Parallel extinction

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q27 - Trophic diversification of Darwins Galapagos island finches

questiontext.text: From an original ancestral seed-eating stock on the Galapagos Islands, Darwin's finches underwent adaptive radiation leading to the evolution of which modified beak types and feeding habits?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Darwin observed that all the varied finches across the Galapagos archipelago evolved locally from an original seed-eating ancestral bird.

Step 2:
Through natural selection favoring exploitation of diverse food sources, altered beak morphologies evolved.

Step 3:
These changes enabled the birds to radiate into distinct trophic niches, notably insectivorous finches and vegetarian finches.

Final Answer:
The original seed-eating finches diversified into insectivorous and vegetarian varieties with altered beaks.

answer.text: Altered beaks enabling diversification into insectivorous and vegetarian finches
Elongated filter-feeding bills identical to those of aquatic flamingos
Tooth-bearing jaws suited for grazing on underwater coral reefs
Carnivorous predatory beaks specialized exclusively for capturing marine mammals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q28 - Diversification of Australian marsupials from ancestral stock

questiontext.text: The remarkable array of Australian marsupials, including the kangaroo, koala, bandicoot, and wombat, illustrates adaptive radiation because they:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Following the geographic isolation of Australia due to continental drift, marsupials faced minimal competition from placental mammals.

Step 2:
From a single ancestral marsupial stock within the Australian continent, numerous distinct marsupial species evolved.

Step 3:
Each evolved distinctive morphological and behavioral traits to occupy different ecological habitats across the island continent.

Final Answer:
A multitude of distinct marsupials evolved from a common ancestral stock within the isolated Australian continent.

answer.text: Evolved through hybridization between placental carnivores and ancient reptilian ancestors
Originated simultaneously across multiple isolated oceanic islands without any shared lineage
All evolved from a single ancestral stock within the Australian island continent to occupy different habitats
Migrated recently from different continents and converged upon identical anatomical structures

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q29 - Phenomenon when multiple adaptive radiations converge

questiontext.text: When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in an isolated geographical area representing different habitats, and distinct lineages evolve remarkably similar morphological forms, the overall phenomenon is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Within an isolated region, multiple lineages may each undergo independent adaptive radiations to fill similar ecological niches.

Step 2:
For example, placental mammals in North America and marsupial mammals in Australia underwent parallel adaptive radiations.

Step 3:
When species from two independent radiating lineages develop similar adaptive features for equivalent ecological roles, the relationship between them represents convergent evolution.

Final Answer:
When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in isolated habitats yielding similar counterparts, it represents convergent evolution.

answer.text: Microevolutionary stasis
Convergent evolution
Artificial selection
Divergent radiation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q30 - Corresponding pairs of placental and marsupial mammals

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs a placental mammal with its convergent Australian marsupial counterpart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Convergent evolution between placental mammals and Australian marsupials produced striking ecological analogs.

Step 2:
Canonical pairs include: Anteater and Numbat (anteater); Flying squirrel and Flying phalanger; Lemur and Spotted cuscus; Bobcat and Tasmanian tiger cat; Wolf and Tasmanian wolf; Mole and Marsupial mole.

Step 3:
Among the given pairs, Anteater and Numbat (anteater) is an exact match.

Final Answer:
Anteater corresponds to Numbat (anteater).

answer.text: Flying squirrel and Tasmanian wolf
Lemur and Flying phalanger

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q31 - Relationship between organismal lifespan and speciation rate

questiontext.text: Why does the evolution of a new variant or species occur within days in bacterial populations, whereas in birds or mammals it requires millions of years?

Natural selection operates over generations as variants with differential reproductive fitness outmultiply others.

The rate of appearance of new forms is directly linked to the life cycle or lifespan of the organism.

Bacteria divide and reproduce within minutes or hours, allowing millions of individuals and multiple generations to elapse in days; organisms with lifespans measured in years take millions of years to achieve equivalent generational turnover.

The rate of appearance of new forms is directly linked to the duration of the life cycle or lifespan.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q32 - Lamarckian hypothesis of use and disuse organs

questiontext.text: Prior to Darwin, the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck explained the evolution of life forms by proposing which mechanism, exemplified by the elongated neck of giraffes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that evolution was driven by the use and disuse of organs.

Step 2:
He argued that ancestral giraffes attempted to forage leaves on tall trees by stretching their necks.

Step 3:
Lamarck asserted that this acquired elongation was transmitted to succeeding generations, gradually producing long-necked modern giraffes (a conjecture subsequently refuted by modern genetics).

Final Answer:
Lamarck proposed the mechanism of use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired characters.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q33 - Genetic foundation underlying adaptive ability and fitness

questiontext.text: According to modern evolutionary synthesis as discussed in the context of Darwinian theory, which statement regarding fitness and adaptation is correct?

Step 1:
Organisms that survive and flourish in hostile or changing environments do so because they possess advantageous characteristics.

Step 2:
Crucially, adaptive ability is not merely a transient physiological response; it is inherited from parents to offspring.

Step 3:
Therefore, adaptive ability has a genetic basis, and reproductive fitness is the end result of an organism's inherited ability to adapt and be selected by nature.

Final Answer:
Adaptive ability is inherited and has a genetic basis, making fitness the end result of adaptation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q37 - Application of binomial expansion in Hardy Weinberg

questiontext.text: In a diploid population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, if the frequency of a recessive allele \(a\) is \(q = 0.4\), what are the expected frequencies of the homozygous dominant genotype (\(AA\)) and the heterozygous genotype (\(Aa\)), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Given that allele frequencies sum to 1 in genetic equilibrium, \(p + q = 1\).

Step 2:
With \(q = 0.4\), the frequency of the dominant allele \(A\) is \(p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6\).

Step 3:
The frequency of homozygous dominant individuals (\(AA\)) is \(p^2 = (0.6)^2 = 0.36\).

Step 4:
The frequency of heterozygous individuals (\(Aa\)) is \(2pq = 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.48\).

Step 5:
The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals (\(aa\)) is \(q^2 = (0.4)^2 = 0.16\), verifying that \(0.36 + 0.48 + 0.16 = 1.00\).

Final Answer:
The expected genotype frequencies are \(0.36\) for \(AA\) and \(0.48\) for \(Aa\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q38 - Five evolutionary factors disrupting Hardy Weinberg equilibrium

questiontext.text: The Hardy-Weinberg genetic equilibrium states that allele frequencies remain constant across generations in the absence of evolutionary influences. Which combination includes all five factors known to disturb this equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Genetic equilibrium requires random mating, large population size, and the absence of evolutionary forces.

Step 2:
Five distinct evolutionary mechanisms alter allele frequencies in a gene pool:

Step 3:
First, gene migration or gene flow (movement of alleles between populations).

Step 4:
Second, genetic drift (random changes in allele frequencies due to chance).

Step 5:
Third, mutation (introduction of novel alleles).

Step 6:
Fourth, genetic recombination (shuffling of alleles during gametogenesis).

Step 7:
Fifth, natural selection (differential reproductive success of genotypes).

Final Answer:
The five factors are gene migration/gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, and natural selection.

answer.text: Branching descent, saltation, use and disuse of organs, biogenesis, and panspermia
Gene migration, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, and natural selection
Random mating, large population size, absence of mutation, absence of migration, and constant climate
Industrial melanism, fossilization, radioactive dating, vegetative propagation, and polyploidy

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q39 - Founder effect resulting from random genetic drift

questiontext.text: When a small group separates from a larger parental population and colonizes a new geographical area, purely by chance their allele frequencies may differ drastically from the original population, occasionally leading to speciation. This phenomenon is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Genetic drift refers to random fluctuations in allele frequencies that occur independently of natural selection, typically having a pronounced effect in small populations.

Step 2:
When an isolated subpopulation becomes established in a new territory, the small colonizing group carries only a sample of the parental gene pool.

Step 3:
Over generations, this new gene pool diverges significantly from the parental stock. The original drifted colonizers become the founders, and this dramatic shift in genetic makeup is known as the founder effect.

Final Answer:
The phenomenon where an original drifted colonizing group establishes a genetically distinct population is termed the founder effect.

answer.text: Adaptive convergence
Founder effect
Stabilising selection
Bottle-neck effect without drift

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q40 - Operation of stabilizing natural selection on traits

questiontext.text: Natural selection can impact phenotypic distribution curves in three distinct ways. When natural selection favors intermediate phenotypes so that more individuals acquire the mean character value, what happens to the phenotypic distribution curve?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Natural selection acts on quantitative phenotypic traits in a population by differential survival of phenotypes.

Step 2:
In stabilizing selection, individuals possessing intermediate phenotypic values survive and reproduce more successfully than individuals with extreme peripheral traits at either end.

Step 3:
As a result of eliminating extreme phenotypes, the distribution peak gets higher and narrower around the mean character value.

Final Answer:
Under stabilizing selection, the peak of the distribution curve gets higher and narrower.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q41 - Contrasting directional selection with disruptive selection curves

questiontext.text: How do directional selection and disruptive selection differ in their effects on the phenotypic distribution curve of a population?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
In directional selection, environmental changes favor phenotypes at one extreme of the distribution over the mean and the opposite extreme, causing the entire peak to shift in one direction.

Step 2:
In disruptive selection, environmental pressures select against the mean character value, favoring individuals at both peripheral ends of the curve.

Step 3:
Consequently, disruptive selection splits the single unimodal distribution into two distinct peaks at the two extremities.

Final Answer:
Directional selection shifts the peak in one direction, while disruptive selection produces two peaks at both peripheral ends.
